newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH GOV PARTIES SEEK COMPROMISE ON SUNDAY OPEN.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH GOV PARTIES SEEK COMPROMISE ON SUNDAY OPEN.

text.p: Parliamentary group leaders of the five parties in Finland's left-right-green government will meet on Friday at 1300 to seek a compromise on a proposal to let retail shops keep open on Sundays, parliament officials said.

The legislature's opening debate on the contested draft bill -- once defeated late last year and reintroduced by Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen, who also turned the issue into a vote of confidence in his cabinet -- started on Thursday evening.
"The government is stable. We will find a compromise and that will be it," Conservative Party parliamentary group leader Ben Zyskowicz told Reuters late on Thursday.

Speeches in parliament by MPs, and media reports on Friday, pointed towards a solution whereby a compromise would be sought on the number of Sundays per year retail stores, hairdessers and barbers will be allowed to hold their doors open for business.
Many government party MPs indicated that it would not make sense to topple the government on a trivial issue like Sunday opening.

Social democratic MP Marjatta Vehkaoja said: "I cannot approve the proposal as it has been given ... I am looking for a compromise because I don't think it would be wise to topple the government like this."
"We must be able to make progress and I am sure we will," Vehkaoja said.
But all back-benchers were not equally convinced that a compromise proposal should be approved and the government be allowed to remain in office.
SDP MP Esa Lahtela said the only kind of compromise he was ready to agree with was that shops would stay closed on Sundays.
"I don't want the government to collapse on this issue, but if it is to happen let it happen," he told parliament.
Parliament's opening debate on the issue is likely to continue on Tuesday, officials at the legislature said.

The economic committee, whose statement -- expected to be built on whatever compromise the coalition parties' parliamentary group leaders reach -- will form the base for voting on the issue, has already started work on the proposal.
The date of the confidence vote has not yet been set.
